content: The individuals listed below contributed to evidence summaries but did not participate in formulating policy recommendations. The following reviewers declared no conflicts of interest that could interfere with the objectives of the guidelines: Modupe Amofa-Seki, Hannah Alsdurf, Rafia Bosan, Jacob Creswell, Cyrus Daneshvar, Ashar Dhana, Pamela Delgado, Brianna Empringham, Helen Feasey, Gregory Fox, Paul Garner, Sifrash Gelaw, Maged Hassan, Mikashmi Kohli, Ramya Kumar, Miranda Langendam, Gary Maartens, Peter Macpherson, Tila Mainga, Lawrence Mwenge, Marriott Nliwasa, Anna Mandalakas, Hector Manzo, Nancy Medley, Fahd Naufal, Zhi Zhen Qin, Maria Ruperez, Adrienne Shapiro, Lily Telisinghe, Anja van ’t Hoog, Kavindhran Velen, Mariana Velleca, Bryan Vonasek, Bada Yang, and Alice Zwerling. A 2019 study by Spruijt et al. evaluated the implementation of latent tuberculosis infection (LTBI) screening and treatment among newly arriving immigrants in the Netherlands using a mixed-methods pilot approach. This study was published in PLOS ONE (14(7): e0219252). The WHO consolidated guidelines on tuberculosis included contributions from various organizations and software providers. For example, AI-based software tools such as Lunit and Delft were made available for research and evaluation purposes since 2016. Additionally, the Observatoire International sur les Impacts Sociétaux de l’Intelligence Artificielle et du Numérique, a publicly funded research observatory in Quebec, provided CAD 159,850 for an interdisciplinary study on the potential health equity impact of computer-aided detection (CAD) from 2020 to 2022. Leila Chaisson disclosed ownership of 230 shares in Merck & Co. Jonathan Golub reported receiving research support, including 20% salary coverage, from the US National Institutes of Health (NIH) for a randomized controlled trial (RCT) titled TB Aftermath. This trial, funded at $500,000 per year for five years, investigates two case-finding strategies to detect recurrent tuberculosis (TB) among individuals who recently completed TB treatment. The trial began in July 2020 in India and is expected to conclude in June 2025. However, the trial's content is not directly related to the PICO questions driving the update of the WHO guidelines. Claudia Denkinger, Sandra Kik, Stefano Ongarello, and Morten Ruhwald disclosed receiving free access to software tools such as qXR, Lunit Insight CXR, and Delft Imaging products for research purposes. These tools were included in the analysis conducted for the WHO TB screening guidelines. Eveline Klinkenberg declared her work with KNCV and consulting on active TB case finding and other TB control aspects. Katherine Robsky reported receiving research support for a project on TB transmission in an urban Ugandan community ($575,698) and funding for her PhD research through the Johns Hopkins Center for Global Health ($3,000 in 2017) and the Fogarty-Fulbright Fellowship ($26,950). She also disclosed systematic review authorship for WHO guidelines on TB screening tests and diagnostic tools, with funding ranging from $6,000 to $35,900 for various projects. Additionally, she received travel support to attend WHO meetings and conferences, as well as a $250 honorarium for participating as faculty in the Advanced TB Diagnostic Research Course at McGill University. Karen Steingart disclosed consulting work and research support related to her reviews for the screening guidelines. She authored systematic reviews on nucleic acid amplification tests (NAATs) for TB and drug-resistant TB detection, as well as other diagnostic tools. She received funding for these reviews, ranging from $3,200 to $35,900, with portions distributed to other team members. She also participated in WHO guideline development groups and received support for attending conferences and purchasing research equipment.
